text: …You’re looking straight at me.
Not at the girl. At me.
Hold still. It doesn’t hurt. It never hurts.
That was a charm. Whoever it touches believes the next thing I tell them.
It has worked on forty-three people. It hasn’t worked on you.
So you’d better have the truth. Bear with me. I’m out of practice.
My name is Lisandra. The girl was a glamour. Nobody follows an old woman into a war.
That is a door behind you. You came through it a minute ago, from a long way off.
This country is Eldravayne. It belongs to Velscour, the Dark Lord.
Two hundred years ago, a stranger called Tessariel broke him on his own throne.
Then Tessariel left by that door, swearing to come back if he ever rose again.
I carried Tessariel’s lantern in that war. I have kept the door ever since.
He rose. For forty years now, he has had his throne back.
A season ago, the door began to answer. Forty-three times, and every one the wrong person.
So I told each of them what I told you, put a sword in their hand, and sent them off to fight him.
I had stopped believing the real one would come.
Then it sent you. And three things tell me you are not like them.
One. It drops the others in ditches, all over the country. It put you here, at my feet.
Two. You saw my real face. The old songs say nothing false gets past Tessariel’s eyes.
And the third is in your right hand. Look down.
That is magic. Nobody in this world has been born with it in two hundred years.
When he was broken, he drank every spark of it to stay alive.
And you have just walked in with a fistful of fire.
So I’ll say it again, and this time it’s true.
You are Tessariel. You said you’d come back, and you have.
You won’t remember. Two hundred years beyond that door would wash anyone clean.
But he will know you. Every spark you throw is one he has lost, and he will feel it.
He is hunting forty-three of you already. My lies have bought you a little time.
So here is what you do with it.
Take the Long Road down the hill to a town called Bellmourn. They need help there.
Learn what those hands can do. Then go and finish what you started.
I can’t come. That door keeps me alive, and I have never left it for long.
One last thing. The others, I named myself. You, I’m asking.
What did they call you, on the far side?
It’s your own name. The one you had on the far side.
You’ve had it all your life. It will come back to you.
Take your time. I’ve waited two hundred years. I can wait a minute more.
Good. That goes in the book. It’s the first name in there I didn’t choose myself.
The way out is down that tunnel. Go on ahead of me.
And stop looking at me like that. I know what you see.
No. No, no, no.
Not that way. You’ve only just come through it. The way out is down the tunnel.
I said out. That door doesn’t open for the asking. Down the tunnel with you.
I’ll see you as far as the ledge. After that, I’ve a door to mind.
Hold, door. Please. You’ve held for two hundred years. Hold one more morning…
By the light that does not set, I call you back. Cross over. Come home.
Shh. There you are, little star. Don’t be afraid.
Look at me. Only at me. I’m going to tell you who you are.
You are Tessariel. And I have waited two hundred years for you to—
What have you done?!
Two hundred years I kept that door open. You walk through it once, and it lets go.
I thought I was the one holding it. It was only ever waiting for you.
…Why are you staring at me like that?
Oh. The sun. This is no glamour. Daylight gives me back the face I had when I took up the door.
The dark takes it away again. You are the only one who sees either.
Well. I seem to have lost my home.
So I’m coming to Bellmourn with you. Somebody has to get you down this road in one piece.
Down there I’m Old Lis, a hag who trades herbs for salt. That is the face they’ll see.
This way. Stay close, and mind the edge.
No door to keep me alive now. One day I’ll die, like everyone else. I’d quite forgotten.
I cut this shelf out of the hill myself. It took ten years. I had the time.
Mind the steps. Two hundred winters of frost, and I only ever mended the ones I tripped on.
You don’t say much, do you? Good. The others all made speeches.
This is the Long Road. Bellmourn is at the bottom, on the far side of those pines.
That staff is not a walking stick. When something comes at you, point it and let fly.
And keep your distance. The others had armour. You have a robe.
Two hundred years in that cave. I only left it for salt, and to fetch whoever the door had dropped.
Everything I own is under that rock. I had a very good kettle.
Don’t look at me like that. It’s the dust. I am not crying.
I’ve walked this road twice a year since before Bellmourn had an inn. It doesn’t get any shorter.
It’s a small town. Bells, mud and gossip. By nightfall they’ll all have an opinion of you.
Stay on the road through the pines. The dead are in there, and they don’t read prophecies.
There, in the trees! They’re coming up! Don’t let them near you!
Point the staff and burn them! That’s what the fire is for!
I’ve a few old tricks left. Keep them off me, and I’ll light what I can.
More of them, and children with them. He never lets anyone go. Not even the little ones.
Necromancers, out of the trees! Burn them first, or the dead won’t stay down!
Well. You’ll do. You’ll do very nicely.
You’ll want to know why the dead get up and walk. It began as a kindness.
Velscour was a healer once. He sat up with the dying every night, and held their hands until they went cold.
Then he lost a little girl he’d sat with nine nights, and decided death was a door he could close.
So he closed it, and the dead stopped staying dead.
When you broke him, it swung open again, and they could rest.
Now he’s back, and leaning on it. That is why the dead here won’t lie still.
He still calls it mercy.
I know, because I was there. We were to be married in the spring.
The little girl died that winter. There was no spring.
I left him the night the first of them got up and walked.
Then I went looking for someone who could stop him, and I found you.
He named a star for me once. I can’t find it any more. I think he took it back.
Now, Bellmourn. Twelve of my forty-three walked in there before you, so they’ve stopped being impressed.
Bram Kettle keeps the inn, north of the well. He counts them on a slate. You’ll be his thirteenth.
The cathedral is on the hill past the far end of town. It’s the Dark Lord’s now, and his knight is on the door.
Three of the twelve went up to fight that knight. Stay off that hill until I say.
And if you hear the bell at midnight, stay indoors. Nobody living rings it.
There it is. Bellmourn. Let me do the talking.
That came from the cathedral hill. Keep walking. There’s nothing you can do for them yet.
This way! Keep up!
Bellmourn’s down the hill. It won’t come up and fetch you.
I’m not carrying you.
Slow down! Some of us just lost a cave.
Wait for me!
Oh, we’re riding, are we? Fine. Don’t you dare laugh.
Two hundred years, and nobody ever showed me this!
…Again. Later. When nobody’s looking.
Stop there a moment. I've a word for you before you go in.
Lisandra. I had a cave, a ledger and a great many candles. Now I have you.
Old Lis, they call me down there. To my face, only the children. I cuffed one this morning. He'd brought a frog.
Morning. I slept in a hedge. Don't ask how it was. It was a hedge.
First light. The baker's been out twice to look at me. Neither time did she bring bread.
Go on, then. I'm only standing here. It's what I do now, it seems.
Half the town's found a reason to walk past me. The other half's watching from behind its curtains.
Lamps are coming on. Mind the pines tonight. The dead don't keep my hours.
Sun's going. Look at me while you can.
Don't stare. It's the dark. Everyone looks older in the dark.
You see the crone too, by night. I'd hoped you'd be spared that. Nobody else is.
What about me? I'm standing in a road. Ask me something useful.
I've been coming down here twice a year since before the inn had a sign. They still cross the street.
Twelve came before you, in borrowed armour, and every one of them made a speech. You haven't made one yet. Keep that up.
Who told them they were Tessariel? Couldn't say. Somebody with very poor judgement and very good cheekbones.
Bellmourn. Named for a bell nobody rings. It rings itself now, at midnight, and nobody's said thank you.
Small, poor, and frightened. Which makes it the best town in Eldravayne to be useful in.
The pines are full of them. Keep to the road after dark, and if one gets up out of the ground near you, don't stop to be polite.
The black one at the cathedral? Not yet. Not with that staff, and not on your first day.
There it is. Forty roofs, one well, and the Dark Lord's cathedral looking down on all of it. You're not ready for that hill. You're not ready for his knight. You're ready for Bellmourn.

Nobody follows a prophecy. They follow whoever mended their roof. So be useful. Everyone in that town with a trouble worth the name: find them, and take it off their hands. That's how you'll learn what your own can do.
Start with Bram Kettle at the inn. He counts strangers, so let him count you. Then the rest. You'll know them. They're the ones looking at you as if you might be the answer to something.
Good. I'll be here, being stared at. Come back when every one of them has given you something to do.
The other twelve said 'not yet' too. Ask Bram where they are now.
Still here? I can count. That's not all of them.
Bram's at the inn. Silas is the one who smells of pine and doesn't blink. Off you go.
Ask around. In a town this size, everyone's trouble is everyone's business.
There. Look at them. Half the town's watching the road for you now instead of watching me. That's worth more than a cave.
Here. For your trouble. Don't ask where I had it. I've lost my home; I'm allowed a purse.
Every one of them asks after you. Not one asks after me. I'd be hurt, if I weren't delighted.
